amerika-vorkolumbisch#sections.2.paragra: The religions of the Americas knew many gods connected with natural forces such as sun, rain, maize and wind. In Mesoamerica a feathered serpent was worshipped for centuries, called Quetzalcoatl by the Aztecs and Kukulkan by the Maya, along with a rain god who appeared as Tlaloc or Chaac. Offerings of blood, food and precious objects were meant to sustain the order of the world; human sacrifice was widespread in many cultures, especially among the Aztecs for the sun and war god Huitzilopochtli. The Inca worshipped the sun god Inti, the earth mother Pachamama and sacred places, the huacas.

Mesoamerica is one of the few regions in the world where writing was invented independently. Early signs are found among the Olmecs and Zapotecs, but only the Maya developed a fully fledged system of word signs and syllable signs with which they wrote down history, myths and rituals. Of their books made of fig-tree bark, only four have survived the Spanish period. The Aztecs used pictorial manuscripts with signs for names, places and numbers. In the Andes there was no writing in the strict sense; information was recorded in knotted cords, the quipus.

Astronomy and mathematics reached a high level. The Maya counted in a base-20 system with a sign for zero and combined a 260-day ritual calendar with a 365-day solar year into a Calendar Round of 52 years. With the Long Count they dated events to the exact day from a mythical starting point in 3114 BC, and they predicted the phases of Venus and eclipses. Many buildings were aligned with sunrises and sunsets, such as the pyramid of Chichén Itzá, on whose staircase a play of shadows resembling a serpent appears at the equinoxes.

Art was varied and often bound up with religion. Olmec colossal heads, the murals of San Bartolo and Bonampak, Maya jade jewelry, Moche portrait vessels and Aztec featherwork are among its masterpieces. The textiles of Paracas and of the Inca are among the finest fabrics of the premodern world. In North America the Hopewell people created figures of mica and copper, and the peoples of the Southwest painted pottery whose traditions live on in today's pueblos.
amerika-vorkolumbisch#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
amerika-vorkolumbisch#sections.3.paragra: The cultures of the Americas achieved their accomplishments without iron, without draft or riding animals – only in the Andes did the llama serve as a pack animal – and without practical use of the wheel, which appears in Mesoamerica only on toy figures. Tools were made of stone, wood, bone and above all obsidian, a volcanic glass that cuts more sharply than steel. Metals such as gold, silver and copper were worked early in the Andes, and later bronze as well; in Mesoamerica metallurgy began only from about AD 600 in western Mexico. That pyramids, cities and road networks nevertheless arose was due to the labor of many people and to sophisticated organization.

Agricultural techniques adapted to very different environments. In the Valley of Mexico the Aztecs created artificial garden islands, the chinampas, in the shallow lakes, which allowed several harvests a year. Maya farmers used terraces, raised fields in swamp areas and water reservoirs, Tiwanaku raised fields with water channels against frost, and the coastal cultures of Peru long irrigation canals that carried water from the Andes into the desert. In Amazonia refuse, charcoal and potsherds created the fertile terra preta over generations.

Trade linked vast areas. Obsidian from central Mexico, jade from Guatemala, cacao from the coastal regions and quetzal feathers were carried over hundreds of kilometers; cacao beans and cotton cloths served as means of payment. In the southwest of today's United States, cacao residues and macaws from Mesoamerica have been found, and the Hopewell network brought copper, shells and obsidian across North America. The Inca empire, by contrast, largely did without markets and money: the state collected produce and labor, stored them in thousands of storehouses and distributed them to the army, workers and the needy.

Building and engineering reached remarkable heights. The Inca fitted stone blocks together without mortar so precisely that their walls withstood earthquakes, and linked their empire with a road network of over 30,000 kilometers, suspension bridges made of grass and relay runners. The Maya built raised causeways between their cities, and the Aztecs aqueducts and dikes in the lakes of the valley. In North America the builders of Cahokia moved millions of baskets of earth for their mounds without draft animals.
antike-griechenland#title: Ancient Greece and the Hellenistic Age
antike-griechenland#summary: Democracy, philosophy, theatre, and the Olympic Games arise in the Greek city-states; Alexander the Great carries Greek culture as far as Egypt and India.
antike-griechenland#overview.0: After the dark centuries that followed the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, hundreds of independent city-states, the poleis, emerged in Greece from about 800 BC. The Greeks adopted the alphabet from the Phoenicians, founded colonies all around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, and were bound together by a shared consciousness through language, gods, the epics of Homer, and the Olympic Games.
antike-griechenland#overview.1: In Athens, through the reforms of Solon and Cleisthenes, a democracy developed in which the assembly of all male citizens made the most important decisions. Sparta, by contrast, was a military state under two kings. In the Persian Wars the Greeks repelled two attacks by the Persian Empire at Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea, which made Athens the leading sea power.
antike-griechenland#overview.2: Under Pericles, Athens experienced a cultural flowering in the 5th century BC, with the building of the Acropolis, the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, the historical writing of Herodotus and Thucydides, and the philosophy of Socrates. The rivalry between Athens and Sparta led to the Peloponnesian War, which ended in 404 BC with the defeat of Athens and permanently weakened the Greek city-states.
antike-griechenland#overview.3: In the 4th century BC Plato and Aristotle founded schools in Athens that shaped European philosophy and science. Politically, Macedonia rose to predominance under Philip II. His son Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire between 334 and 323 BC and pushed as far as Egypt and India. His early death left behind an empire that his generals divided among themselves.
antike-griechenland#overview.4: In the Hellenistic age Greek and oriental culture merged. Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean, and Alexandria with its library became the centre of scholarship. One after another Rome subjugated the Hellenistic kingdoms; in 146 BC Greece became Roman, and with the death of Cleopatra in 30 BC Egypt was the last to fall to Rome.
antike-griechenland#consequences.0: Athenian democracy is the first known example of rule by the people and the point of reference for all modern democracies.
antike-griechenland#consequences.1: The philosophy, logic, mathematics, medicine, and historical writing of the Greeks form the foundation of European science.
antike-griechenland#consequences.2: Greek theatre, epic, lyric poetry, and sculpture set standards by which art and literature are still guided today.
antike-griechenland#consequences.3: Through Alexander's conquests and the Hellenistic age, the Greek language and culture spread as far as Egypt, Persia, and India; the New Testament was written in Greek.
antike-griechenland#consequences.4: The Romans took over Greek education, art, and the world of the gods and passed them on to medieval and modern Europe.
antike-griechenland#keyFacts.0: Between 750 and 550 BC Greek cities found hundreds of colonies from Spain to the Black Sea.
antike-griechenland#keyFacts.1: In 594 BC Solon reforms Athens and abolishes debt bondage; in 508 BC Cleisthenes lays the foundation of democracy.
antike-griechenland#keyFacts.2: In 480 BC Leonidas and 300 Spartans fall at Thermopylae; in the same year the Greeks win at Salamis.
antike-griechenland#keyFacts.3: In 472 BC The Persians by Aeschylus, the oldest surviving tragedy, is performed; in 447 BC construction of the Parthenon begins.
antike-griechenland#keyFacts.4: Around 400 BC Hippocrates and his school on Kos establish medicine as a science with natural causes.
antike-griechenland#keyFacts.5: In 331 BC Alexander founds Alexandria; after his death in 323 BC the Diadochi divide his empire in wars lasting until 281 BC.
antike-griechenland#keyFacts.6: In 212 BC Archimedes dies during the capture of Syracuse by the Romans; the science of the Hellenistic age lives on in Alexandria.
antike-griechenland#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
antike-griechenland#sections.0.paragraph: The Greek polis knew almost all the forms of government that political theory later described: kingship, aristocracy, tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy. In the 7th and 6th centuries BC tyrants seized power in many cities, often with the support of the people against the nobility; in Athens, Peisistratus and his sons promoted festivals, buildings, and farmers until Hippias was driven out in 510 BC. The word tyrant acquired its negative ring only later.

Athenian democracy rested on the popular assembly, which decided on war, peace, laws, and finances, on the Council of 500 filled by lot, and on jury courts with hundreds of judges. Almost all offices were allotted and filled anew each year; only the ten generals were elected, which is why Pericles directed policy through that office for decades. Women, slaves, and the numerous immigrants, the metics, remained excluded; citizens made up about one tenth of the inhabitants.

Sparta, by contrast, was governed by two kings, a council of elders, and five ephors elected annually; the full citizens lived as professional warriors off the land, which was worked by the unfree helots. After the Peloponnesian War, Sparta, Thebes, and Athens alternated as the leading power until Philip II of Macedonia subjugated the Greeks at Chaeronea in 338 BC. In the Hellenistic age kings such as the Ptolemies and the Seleucids ruled over vast empires, while the poleis retained only limited self-government.
antike-griechenland#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
antike-griechenland#sections.1.paragraph: The life of an Athenian family took place in a simple house with an inner courtyard; the men spent the day in the agora, in the gymnasion, or in the popular assembly, while the women of the citizen class ran the household, wove, and left the house mainly for religious festivals. Girls were married off at about 15 years of age, and boys learned reading, writing, music, and sport. In Sparta, by contrast, girls were trained physically, and women could own land.

Without slaves the Greek economy would have been inconceivable: they worked in households, workshops, in the fields, and under cruel conditions in the silver mines of Laurion, from which Athens financed its fleet. The symposion, the men's drinking party with conversation, songs, and games, was the centre of social life; hospitality was regarded as a sacred duty. Women such as Sappho on Lesbos or the educated Aspasia in Athens show that there were exceptions to the male-dominated order as well.

Sport and competition ran through Greek culture. Besides Olympia there were the games at Delphi, Corinth, and Nemea; victors were celebrated like heroes in their home cities and praised by poets such as Pindar. Theatre performances, music, and rhetoric were also competitions. The agon, the contest, shaped the idea that a person should distinguish himself through achievement.
antike-griechenland#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
antike-griechenland#sections.2.paragraph: The Greeks venerated Zeus, Athena, Apollo, and the other Olympians with sacrifices, processions, and festivals; every polis had its patron deity, and the temples on the Acropolis or at Delphi were magnificent buildings of marble. Cities and kings consulted the oracle of Delphi before wars and the founding of colonies; its ambiguous answers became proverbial. Mystery cults such as the one at Eleusis promised initiates a better life after death.

Out of the festivals of Dionysus, theatre arose in Athens: tragedies by Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides dealt with guilt, fate, and justice before thousands of spectators, while the comedies of Aristophanes mocked politicians and philosophers. Herodotus founded historical writing by asking after the causes of the Persian Wars, and Thucydides turned it into a critical analysis of power. The sculptors Phidias, Polykleitos, and Praxiteles created the ideal of the human body that Rome and the Renaissance took over.

From the 6th century BC the natural philosophers of Ionia sought natural explanations of the world instead of divine ones. Pythagoras and Euclid created mathematics based on proof, Hippocrates medicine, Aristotle biology and logic. In Alexandria, Eratosthenes calculated the circumference of the earth, Aristarchus supposed that the earth orbits the sun, and Archimedes discovered the laws of the lever and of buoyancy. This science was passed on to the Middle Ages through Byzantium and the Arab world.
antike-griechenland#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
antike-griechenland#sections.3.paragraph: Mountainous, barren Greece fed its inhabitants with barley, olives, wine, and goats only with difficulty; shortage of land drove many cities to found colonies and to import grain from Sicily, Egypt, and the Black Sea region. In return Athens exported olive oil, wine, silver, and the painted vases of its pottery workshops, which today stand in all the great museums.

Around 600 BC the Greeks adopted the coin from Lydia and spread it across the entire Mediterranean; the Athenian silver owl became the most important trading currency. The harbour of Piraeus was the largest trading hub of the Aegean, with banks, warehouses, and shipyards. The triremes, warships with three banks of oars and 170 rowers, secured maritime trade and the power of Athens.

In the Hellenistic age cities such as Alexandria, Antioch, and Pergamon grew into metropolises with hundreds of thousands of inhabitants, planned street grids, water pipes, and libraries. Engineers developed catapults, cranes, the Archimedes screw for raising water, and forerunners of the steam engine, which however remained curiosities. The lighthouse of Pharos, one of the Seven Wonders of the World, showed ships the way into the harbour of Alexandria, through which grain from the Nile delta reached the whole Mediterranean world.
rom#summary: From a small city on the Tiber to a world empire around the Mediterranean: Rome shaped the law, language, urban planning, and politics of Europe for centuries.
rom#overview.0: According to legend, Rome was founded by Romulus in 753 BC. In fact the city grew out of several villages on the hills by the Tiber and was at first governed by kings. Around 509 BC the Romans drove out their last king and established a republic in which annually elected consuls, the Senate, and the popular assemblies shared power.
rom#overview.1: In the following centuries Rome subjugated first Italy and then, in the Punic Wars against Carthage, the western Mediterranean. Greece, Asia Minor, Gaul, and Egypt followed. The conquests brought enormous wealth, but also social tensions: smallholders were impoverished, slaves worked on large estates, and ambitious generals such as Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar used their legions for their own ends.
rom#overview.2: After civil wars and the murder of Caesar, his adoptive son Octavian established the principate as Augustus from 27 BC: formally the republic continued to exist, but in fact an emperor ruled. The Pax Romana of the first two centuries AD brought peace, trade, roads, aqueducts, and flourishing cities from Britain to Syria.
rom#overview.3: From the 3rd century onwards the empire fell into a crisis of civil wars, inflation, and attacks on the frontiers. Diocletian and Constantine reformed the administration and the army; Constantine promoted Christianity, which became the state religion in 380. In 395 the empire was finally divided into a western and an eastern half.
rom#overview.4: The Western Roman Empire disintegrated under the pressure of the migration of peoples. In 476 the Germanic military leader Odoacer deposed the last Western Roman emperor, Romulus Augustulus. The Eastern Roman Empire with its capital Constantinople continued to exist as Byzantium for almost another thousand years.
rom#consequences.0: Roman law forms the basis of many European legal systems to this day.
rom#consequences.1: Out of Latin arose the Romance languages Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Romanian; Latin terms shape science and the church.
rom#consequences.2: Roads, cities, aqueducts, and building forms such as the arch, the dome, and concrete permanently influenced the architecture and infrastructure of Europe.
rom#consequences.3: Christianity spread throughout the Roman Empire and became the defining religion of Europe.
rom#consequences.4: The idea of a Roman imperial office lived on in the Holy Roman Empire and in the titles emperor and tsar.
rom#keyFacts.0: Around 450 BC Roman law is set down in writing for the first time in the Twelve Tables.
rom#keyFacts.1: From 73 to 71 BC the slave revolt of Spartacus shakes Italy; in 31 BC the naval battle of Actium decides the civil war in Octavian's favour.
rom#keyFacts.2: In AD 80 the Colosseum is opened; under Trajan the empire reaches its greatest extent in 117, from Britain to Mesopotamia.
rom#keyFacts.3: In 212 the emperor Caracalla grants Roman citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire through the Constitutio Antoniniana.
rom#keyFacts.4: From 235 to 284 the empire experiences the Crisis of the Third Century, with more than 20 emperors, civil wars, and inflation; Diocletian reorganizes it from 284.
rom#keyFacts.5: In 325 the Council of Nicaea under Constantine lays down the foundations of the Christian creed.
rom#keyFacts.6: In 410 the Visigoths under Alaric sack Rome, in 451 Attila's Huns are stopped at the Catalaunian Plains, and in 476 the Western Roman Empire comes to an end.
rom#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
rom#sections.0.paragraphs.0: The constitution of the republic rested on the distribution of power among magistrates who changed annually, the Senate as the council of former officeholders, and the popular assemblies. The Conflict of the Orders between the aristocratic patricians and the plebeians led over two centuries to the Twelve Tables, to the tribunes of the people with their right of veto, and finally to the opening of all offices. Abroad, Rome bound the defeated cities of Italy to itself through graded alliances and citizenship rights and was thus able to draw on enormous reserves of troops.
rom#sections.0.paragraphs.1: The conquest of the Mediterranean world overtaxed the institutions of a city republic. Governors enriched themselves in the provinces, generals such as Marius, Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar commanded armies that were personally loyal to them, and politics was determined by violence, bribery, and civil wars. The principate of Augustus solved the problem by concentrating power over the army and the provinces in one hand while at the same time preserving the Senate and republican forms.
rom#sections.0.paragraphs.2: The imperial period knew no fixed law of succession, which is why adoption, the army, and the Praetorian Guard decided who followed. In the 2nd century the adoptive emperors from Nerva to Marcus Aurelius brought stability; in the 3rd century the legions proclaimed dozens of soldier emperors. Diocletian divided rule among four rulers in the tetrarchy, introduced the court ceremonial of oriental kings, and founded the dominate, in which the emperor appeared as lord and god. Constantine and his successors joined this form of rule to Christianity.
rom#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
rom#sections.1.paragraphs.0: Roman society was strictly graded: senators, equestrians, free citizens, freedmen, and slaves. The family stood under the almost unlimited authority of the father of the house, yet Roman women could own property, obtain a divorce, and, like Livia or Agrippina, exercise considerable influence at the imperial court. The system of clientage bound wealthy patrons and their clients together in a network of protection and allegiance.
rom#sections.1.paragraphs.1: In the Italy of the late republic slaves made up a third of the population; they toiled on country estates, in mines, and in households, but were also physicians, teachers, and administrators. Revolts such as that of Spartacus were put down with the utmost severity, yet slaves could also be freed and their children obtain citizenship. In 212 the Constitutio Antoniniana made almost all free inhabitants of the empire Romans.
rom#sections.1.paragraphs.2: Life in Rome, a city of a million people, took place in cramped tenement blocks, in markets, in the baths, and at the games. Free grain and entertainment, bread and circuses, secured the quiescence of the masses; in the Colosseum gladiators and animals died before 50,000 spectators, and in the Circus Maximus hundreds of thousands thrilled to chariot races. The provincial cities from Britain to Syria imitated the model of Rome with a forum, temples, a theatre, and baths, as Pompeii shows.
rom#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
rom#sections.2.paragraphs.0: The Romans adopted the Greek gods under Latin names and supplemented them with deities of their own such as Janus and the household gods. Religion was a matter of state: colleges of priests, sacrifices, and omens accompanied every political act, and the imperial cult bound the provinces to Rome. Alongside this, mystery cults from the East spread, such as the worship of Isis and of Mithras, and from Judaea came Christianity, which survived the persecutions under Nero, Decius, and Diocletian and rose to become the state religion in the 4th century.
rom#sections.2.paragraphs.1: In literature and philosophy the Romans followed Greek models and yet created something of their own: Virgil's Aeneid as a national epic, the odes of Horace, the historical works of Livy and Tacitus, the satires of Juvenal. Stoicism shaped Roman ideas of duty and composure; Seneca and the emperor Marcus Aurelius left behind philosophical writings that are still read today. The Council of Nicaea in 325 showed how theology became an affair of the empire.
rom#sections.2.paragraphs.2: Rome's real achievement lay in law and organization. Jurists such as Gaius and Ulpian developed civil law into a system that the emperor Justinian had codified in the 6th century and whose influence continues to this day. Education rested on grammar and rhetoric; in Alexandria scholars such as the mathematician Hypatia were still active in late antiquity, and her murder in 415 announced the end of ancient science.
rom#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
rom#sections.3.paragraphs.0: The Mediterranean was the Mare Nostrum, our sea, across which grain from Egypt and North Africa, oil from Spain, wine from Italy and Gaul, marble from Greece, and luxury goods from India and China flowed to Rome. The harbour of Ostia and the state-organized grain supply fed the capital. A uniform currency, safe sea routes after the destruction of the pirates by Pompey, and a legal system for contracts made the empire into an enormous economic area.
rom#sections.3.paragraphs.1: Some 80,000 kilometres of paved roads connected the provinces with Rome, built by legionaries for troops, messengers, and merchants. Aqueducts carried water over dozens of kilometres into the cities, and concrete made from volcanic ash allowed domes such as that of the Pantheon and harbour structures built under water. Water wheels, cranes, underfloor heating, and glass windows belonged to the state of the art; Hadrian's Wall and the limes showed how engineering secured frontiers.
rom#sections.3.paragraphs.2: In the 3rd century this system partly broke down: emperors reduced the silver content of the coinage in order to pay soldiers, prices exploded, and trade and cities suffered from civil wars and invasions. In 301 Diocletian tried in vain to impose maximum prices, and he bound peasants and craftsmen to their occupations. In the West the economy shifted to large estates, whose dependent coloni later became the peasants of the Middle Ages.
asien-altertum#title: The Empires of Asia: Persia, India, China, Japan
asien-altertum#summary: While Greeks and Romans ruled in Europe, great empires, world religions, and inventions such as paper and the compass arose in Asia and shape the world to this day.
asien-altertum#overview.0: Around 550 BC Cyrus II united the Persians and the Medes and within a few decades created the largest empire in history up to that time. It reached from the Aegean to the Indus and was held together by satrapies, royal roads, and a policy of religious tolerance. In 330 BC Alexander the Great conquered the Persian Empire, yet Persian culture and administration lived on in the succeeding empires of the Parthians and the Sasanians.
asien-altertum#overview.1: At the same time new teachings arose in India and China that determine Asian thought to this day. Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught a way to overcome suffering in northern India, while Confucius in China devised an ethics of duty, education, and order. The Maurya king Ashoka made Buddhism the religion of a great empire in the 3rd century BC and sent missionaries as far as Sri Lanka.
asien-altertum#overview.2: In China, Qin Shi Huangdi ended the period of the Warring States in 221 BC and created a unified empire with a common script, currency, and system of measures. The succeeding Han dynasty ruled for four centuries, opened the Silk Road to the West, and raised Confucianism to the status of state doctrine. Under the Han, paper, the compass, and an administration of officials filled by examination also came into being.
asien-altertum#overview.3: Under the Gupta dynasty in the 4th and 5th centuries India experienced a golden age of mathematics, astronomy, poetry, and art; it was here that the decimal system with zero arose. Under the Tang dynasty from 618 onwards China reached a new peak: the capital Chang'an was the largest city in the world, and trade and Buddhism connected China with Central Asia, Korea, and Japan.
asien-altertum#overview.4: Japan adopted writing, Buddhism, and administration from China and, in the Heian period from 794, developed a courtly culture of its own with a syllabic script and novels. In Southeast Asia the Khmer built Angkor Wat, the largest temple complex in the world, in the 12th century. In this period the empires of Asia were often larger, richer, and technically more advanced than those of Europe.
asien-altertum#consequences.0: Buddhism, Confucianism, and Hinduism still shape the religion, ethics, and society of billions of people in Asia.
asien-altertum#consequences.1: China's unification under Qin Shi Huangdi created the basis for a state that endured for more than two thousand years despite many changes of dynasty.
asien-altertum#consequences.2: Paper, the compass, gunpowder, and printing travelled from China westwards along the Silk Road and changed science, warfare, and education worldwide.
asien-altertum#consequences.3: The Indian decimal system with zero was transmitted to Europe through the Arab world and is the basis of our mathematics today.
asien-altertum#consequences.4: The Persian model of a multi-ethnic empire with provinces, roads, and religious tolerance influenced Alexander, Rome, and the later Islamic empires.
asien-altertum#keyFacts.0: Around 500 BC Buddhism, Confucianism, and Daoism emerge, three teachings that shape Asian thought to this day.
asien-altertum#keyFacts.1: In 221 BC Qin Shi Huangdi unifies China; his Terracotta Army, discovered in 1974, numbers around 8,000 clay soldiers.
asien-altertum#keyFacts.2: Around 100 BC Sima Qian completes the Shiji, the first comprehensive work of Chinese historical writing.
asien-altertum#keyFacts.3: In 224 Ardashir I founds the Sasanian Empire, which rules Persia until the Arab conquest in 651.
asien-altertum#keyFacts.4: From 690 to 705 Wu Zetian reigns as the only woman in the history of China to rule as empress in her own right.
asien-altertum#keyFacts.5: In 868 the Diamond Sutra is produced, the oldest surviving printed book bearing a date.
asien-altertum#keyFacts.6: Around 1008 the lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu completes the Tale of Genji in Japan, the first novel in world literature.
asien-altertum#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
asien-altertum#sections.0.paragraphs.0: The Chinese emperors justified their rule with the Mandate of Heaven: a just ruler governs with divine approval, an unjust one loses it and may be overthrown. Natural disasters, famines, and revolts were therefore regarded as warning signs from Heaven. This way of thinking explained why dynasties such as the Qin, the Han, or the Tang rose and fell again, and it allowed every successful rebel to present himself as the new bearer of the mandate. Even Wu Zetian, the only empress in her own right, had her rule confirmed by Buddhist scriptures and omens.
asien-altertum#sections.0.paragraphs.1: Unlike the aristocratic states of Europe, China had relied since the Han on a body of officials selected through examinations on the Confucian classics. Under the Tang, and especially under Wu Zetian, this system was extended, so that men from more modest families could also rise to high office. The officials administered taxes, granaries, canals, and courts in the provinces and were transferred regularly so that they could not build up a power base of their own. The model was adopted by Korea, Japan, and Vietnam.
